name: Additive Color
statement: Mix red, green, and blue light and you build up every colour, ending in white.
statementAccent: you build up every colour, ending in white
meaning: Additive color is the mixing of coloured light, in which colours are created by adding light of different wavelengths together. Starting from darkness, black, adding light produces colour, and adding more light makes the result brighter, until combining all the primaries yields white. The additive primary colours are red, green, and blue, from which the initials RGB come. Combining them in pairs gives the secondary colours: red and green make yellow, green and blue make cyan, and blue and red make magenta, while all three together make white. Additive color is the way light sources and electronic displays produce colour: televisions, computer and phone screens, and other displays give each pixel red, green, and blue elements whose emitted light adds together to make the perceived colour. It is the opposite of subtractive color, the mixing of pigments and inks. Additive color works because human vision is trichromatic, so mixing three primaries of light can reproduce a wide range of colours.
mechanism: Additive color mixing combines beams of coloured light so their wavelengths add. Because it begins in darkness and each added light contributes brightness, the more light of more colours is combined, the lighter and whiter the result, culminating in white when red, green, and blue light are combined at full intensity. The choice of red, green, and blue as primaries reflects the physiology of the eye: human colour vision is trichromatic, with three types of cone photoreceptors roughly most sensitive to long, medium, and short wavelengths, which correspond to red, green, and blue. By adjusting the relative intensities of three primary lights that each strongly stimulate one cone type, a display can produce cone responses that the brain interprets as almost any colour, a huge range of hues from just three primaries. This is why screens are built from red, green, and blue subpixels: at a distance their emitted light blends additively, and varying the brightness of each subpixel across the image reproduces full-colour pictures. Additive mixing thus ties the physics of light to the three-channel structure of human vision.

examples.text: Televisions and phone screens give each pixel red, green, and blue elements whose emitted light adds to produce the perceived colour.
Red and green light make yellow, green and blue make cyan, blue and red make magenta, and all three together make white.
Theatrical lighting mixes coloured light sources additively, so overlapping beams of different colours combine and brighten toward white.

variants.name: The RGB primaries
variants.text: Red, green, and blue, the additive primary colours from which coloured light and displays build all other colours.

variants.name: Trichromatic basis
variants.text: The grounding of additive color in the eye's three cone types, so three primaries suffice to reproduce most colours.

whyItMatters: Additive color is fundamental to how light and modern technology produce colour, underlying every screen and display we use. Because televisions, monitors, phones, cameras, and projectors all create colour by mixing red, green, and blue light, understanding additive mixing is essential to imaging, display engineering, digital photography, and design, where colours are specified in RGB values. The principle also illuminates the nature of colour itself: that a vast range of hues can be produced from just three primaries because human vision reduces light to three channels. Additive color contrasts sharply with subtractive color, the mixing of pigments and inks that starts from white and darkens, and knowing which regime applies, light or pigment, is crucial for anyone working with colour across media, since the same colour behaves differently on screen and in print. Grounded in the trichromatic structure of the eye, additive color connects the physics of light, the physiology of vision, and the technology of displays, making it a cornerstone concept in colour science and digital media.

working.text: begin with no light, black, so that adding coloured light builds colour and brightness.
combine red, green, and blue light in varying intensities to stimulate the eye's three cone types.
let more combined light brighten the result, reaching white when all three primaries combine at full intensity.

limits: Additive color describes the mixing of light, not pigments, so it does not model how inks and paints behave, which follow subtractive color and darken as colorants are added; applying the wrong model leads to error when moving between screen and print. The specific primaries and the range of reproducible colours, the gamut, depend on the exact red, green, and blue used, so no set of three primaries can reproduce every colour the eye can see. Additive color rests on the trichromatic simplification of vision, so it works because the eye reduces spectra to three signals, but this also means displays reproduce colours metamerically, matching appearance rather than physical spectra.
misreadings: Additive color does not describe mixing paints; mixing coloured light adds toward white, while mixing pigments subtracts toward dark, so the two regimes are opposite. Combining all the additive primaries does not make black but white, since each adds light. And three primaries do not reproduce literally every possible colour, only a wide gamut, so treating light mixing like paint mixing, expecting all colours to darken toward black, or assuming three primaries cover the entire spectrum, misreads a system in which coloured lights add and brighten toward white.
origin: A foundational concept in colour science: the mixing of coloured light, with red, green, and blue primaries adding toward white, grounded in the trichromatic Young-Helmholtz theory of vision and used in all electronic displays.
